message.content: Lions (family Felidae, order Carnivora) and zebras (family Equidae, order Perissodactyla) share a very distant common ancestor – the last common ancestor of the two orders Carnivora and Perissodactyla, which belongs to the larger clade **Laurasiatheria**. This ancestor lived roughly 70–80 million years ago, long before the diversification of modern felids and equids.

The user asks: "What is the common ancestor of lion and zebra?" They want an answer. There's no tool needed. Just respond with the common ancestor. The common ancestor of lion (Panthera leo) and zebra (Equus quagga) would be something like the last common ancestor of the family Felidae and Equidae. That would be a more distant ancestor, maybe from the order Carnivora vs Perissodactyla. Actually lions are in the order Carnivora, suborder Feliformia. Zebras are in the order Perissodactyla. So their common ancestor would be at the level of the clade Euarchontoglires? Wait, let's think.

Lion: Kingdom Animalia, Phylum Chordata, Class Mammalia, Order Carnivora, Family Felidae. Zebra: Kingdom Animalia, Phylum Chordata, Class Mammalia, Order Perissodactyla, Family Equidae. So the common ancestor is at the level of the class Mammalia. But we can get more specific: The last common ancestor of the orders Carnivora and Perissodactyla would be within the clade Laurasiatheria. Within Laurasiatheria, the two orders diverged early. So the common ancestor might be the last common ancestor of the clades Carnivora and Perissodactyla, which is the last common ancestor of the group called Laurasiatheria. So the answer could be "Laurasiatheria" or "the last common ancestor of the Laurasiatherian mammals." Or simply "Mammals." But perhaps they want the most recent common ancestor: the last common ancestor of the families Felidae and Equidae is the last common ancestor of the orders Carnivora and Perissodactyla, which is the last common ancestor of the clade Laurasiatheria. So I'd answer: The last common ancestor of lions and zebras is the last common ancestor of the Laurasiatherian mammals, which lived around 70 million years ago. Alternatively, if they want a species name, it's not known; it's a hypothetical ancestor. So I'd say: It's the last common ancestor of the orders Carnivora and Perissodactyla, part of the clade Laurasiatheria. So answer accordingly.
